title: Vapour Condensers on Brew Kettles | Craft Beer School
desc: How a kettle vapour condenser recovers boil heat, cuts brewery odour and what to watch: vacuum risk, condensate handling and cleaning.
teaser: Every litre boiled off is 2.26 MJ going up the stack. A vapour condenser brings much of it back as hot water.
standfirst: A vapour condenser captures steam from the kettle and turns it back into water, recovering the heat in the process. It saves energy and quietens the smell of brew day for neighbours. It also brings a few risks worth understanding.
sections:
During the boil, steam rises from the kettle and normally leaves through a stack to the outside. A vapour condenser places a heat exchanger in that path. Cold water flows through it, the steam condenses on the cold surface and gives up its latent heat. The water leaves the condenser hot and goes to a hot water tank.

The condensed vapour, called condensate, drains away separately. It carries the volatile compounds the boil was meant to remove, including DMS and some hop oils.

Condensing steam releases about 2,257 kJ per kg. Worked example: a 1,000 litre batch with 8% evaporation produces 80 litres of steam. Condensing all of it releases about 181 MJ.

That energy could heat roughly 700 litres of water from 20 °C to 80 °C, since 181,000 kJ divided by (4.19 kJ/kg °C x 60 °C) is about 716 kg. In practice recovery is lower because of losses, but it is still a large share of the energy spent boiling off water. Our guide to where heat is lost in a brewhouse shows how this fits into the full energy picture.

The smell of a boil travels. In mixed use areas, which describes many Indian brewpubs in malls and commercial streets, brew day smells can cause complaints. A vapour condenser captures most of the odour compounds in the condensate rather than releasing them into the air.

This alone justifies a condenser for some sites, even before counting the energy saving.
Never let condensate return to the kettle

The condensate holds DMS and other volatiles the boil drove off. If it drains back into the kettle, those compounds go straight back into the wort and the boil achieves less. The condensate line must slope away from the kettle and drain freely to a collection point or drain.

Check the design carefully. A sagging pipe or a blocked drain can send condensate back into the stack and down into the wort without anyone noticing, until DMS shows up in the beer. Our guide to DMS in pale lager explains why this matters.

When steam condenses, its volume collapses. If a condenser removes steam faster than the kettle produces it, pressure in the kettle can drop below atmospheric. A kettle is not usually designed for vacuum. In the worst case it can deform or collapse.

The same risk appears at the end of the boil when heat is cut but cold water keeps flowing through the condenser. Designs include vacuum relief valves or open vents to let air in. Check that these are present, clean and unblocked. Turn off condenser water when the boil ends, before the kettle cools.

Vapour carries hop oils, protein fragments and other organics that coat the condenser surfaces over time. A fouled condenser recovers less heat and can harbour microbes. Include the condenser in your CIP plan, with caustic to remove organic soil and acid if scale forms on the water side.

Check the water side as well. Hard borewell water used as cooling water can leave scale that reduces heat transfer. Softened water or regular descaling keeps performance up.
Energy storage and the rest of the brewhouse

A condenser produces most of its hot water during the boil, which may not match when that water is needed. Larger brewhouses link the condenser to an energy storage tank. Stored hot water is then used to preheat the next wort on its way from the lauter tun to the kettle, which closes the loop and cuts the energy needed to reach the boil.

Small breweries usually run simpler systems that send hot water to the hot liquor tank for cleaning and the next mash. That works if the hot liquor tank has room. If it already fills from knockout, extra hot water from the condenser may overflow and be wasted.

Before buying, map hot water use across a brew day. Note how much hot water comes from knockout, how much the condenser would add and how much the brewery actually uses. If supply already exceeds demand, invest in better use of the hot water you have first.

A condenser costs money to buy and install. The payback depends on how often you brew, your energy price and whether you can use all the hot water it produces. A brewery that already overflows its hot liquor tank at knockout may not need more hot water.

Working through this kind of energy and design trade off is part of the brewhouse engineering we cover on the advanced course.

Your first step: calculate the steam you boil off in a week, multiply by 2.26 MJ per litre and see what it would mean in fuel saved.
faqs: How does a vapour condenser save energy?
It condenses kettle steam on a cold surface, recovering the latent heat into water that can be used elsewhere in the brewery.
Can condensate go back into the kettle?
No. It contains DMS and other volatiles the boil removed, so it must drain away from the kettle.
Can a vapour condenser damage a kettle?
It can if it creates a vacuum. Vacuum relief and shutting off condenser water at the end of the boil prevent this.
